title: Sublimation vs Screen Printing vs Heat Transfer for Basketball Jerseys
description: The three ways a design gets onto a basketball jersey, what each one actually does to the fabric, and which one fails first.
standfirst: Three processes, three completely different things happening to the fabric — and three different ways a jersey ends up looking tired by January.

paras: The three methods are not variations on a theme. They put the design in genuinely different places, and everything about how a jersey ages follows from that one difference.

Dye sublimation turns solid dye directly into a gas under heat and pressure, and that gas bonds with the polyester at a molecular level. The design does not sit on the jersey — it becomes part of the fiber. Run a fingernail across a sublimated number and you feel fabric, not a raised edge. This is how every sublimated basketball jersey we produce is made.

Screen printing pushes ink through a mesh stencil onto the surface of the fabric, one screen per color. The ink cures as a thin layer sitting on top of the cloth. It is durable for what it is, but it is a layer, and layers can crack.

Heat transfer, usually vinyl, cuts a shape from a colored film and presses it onto the garment with heat and adhesive. It is the fastest method and the one most local shops use for numbers, and it is also the one with the shortest life.

A vinyl number is the first to go. It fails at the edges and at fold lines, typically somewhere between twenty and forty washes, and once an edge lifts the rest follows quickly. On a jersey worn twice a week through a season, that is January.

A screen print lasts longer but cracks eventually, because the cured ink is less flexible than the fabric under it. Every stretch works the layer slightly, and a design across a chest gets stretched on every rebound.

Sublimation has no failure mode of this kind at all, because there is nothing on the surface to fail. What eventually retires a sublimated jersey is the fabric wearing out, which is the right way round — the garment should outlive the graphic or they should go together, not the graphic first.
sections.pull: The question is not which print looks best on day one. All three look fine on day one. The question is what the jersey looks like in the last game of the season.

paras: Screen printing charges per color, because each color is a separate screen, a separate setup and a separate pass. A four-color crest costs four times the setup of a one-color one, which is why school jerseys have historically had simple designs — the constraint was economic, not aesthetic.

Sublimation lays the entire design down in one pass regardless of how many colors it contains. A twelve-color design with a gradient and a photographic fill costs exactly what a two-color design costs, and every jersey in a run can carry a different name at no extra charge because each is printed from its own file rather than a shared screen.

That is also why short runs work. Fifteen jerseys with no setup charge is a genuinely different economic proposition from fifteen jerseys with four screens to burn, which is what makes a one-night awareness game kit affordable rather than a fundraising problem of its own.
Two real limits, and both are worth knowing before you commit.

It only works on polyester. The dye needs a polymer to bond with, and there is nothing in cotton for it to enter. A cotton or cotton-blend garment cannot be sublimated at all, whatever a supplier tells you.

And it prints light to dark. You cannot sublimate a pale design onto an already-dark garment, because the process adds color rather than replacing it. A dark ground is produced by dyeing the whole panel, which is a different job — and it is why a black jersey with light numerals is printed rather than simply dyed.

sections.h2: When a heat transfer is still the right call
paras: There is one situation where vinyl genuinely wins, and it is timing. If your roster is not settled, you cannot order numbered jerseys — but you can order blanks now, hold them, and have a local shop number them the week the squad is final.
That is exactly what undecorated blank jerseys are for, and it is why they ship faster than anything else we make: there is no artwork stage and nothing to proof.

One warning to pass to whoever does the pressing. Polyester dye-migrates under high heat, and a red or navy garment pressed too hot will bleed dye into white vinyl over the following weeks, turning the lettering pink. A low-temperature transfer avoids it completely, and any shop that regularly works with athletic polyester will know the setting.

faqs.q: Does a sublimated jersey feel different from a screen-printed one?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the easiest way to tell them apart. A sublimated design has no texture at all — the fabric feels identical where the number is and where it is not. A screen print or a vinyl number is a raised layer you can feel with a fingernail, and on a large chest graphic you can feel that it is less flexible than the cloth around it.

faqs.q: Can you sublimate onto a cotton jersey?
faqs.a: No. The process works by dye bonding into a polymer, and cotton has nothing for it to bond with. Any supplier offering a sublimated cotton jersey is either using a blend with enough polyester to take a washed-out result, or applying a transfer and calling it sublimation.

faqs.q: Is sublimation more expensive?
faqs.a: Not for anything with more than one or two colors. Screen printing charges per color because each is a separate screen and setup; sublimation charges per garment regardless of color count. A simple two-color design on a large run can be cheaper to screen print, and almost nothing else is.

faqs.q: How long does a sublimated jersey last?
faqs.a: Until the fabric wears out, which is the point. There is nothing on the surface to crack, peel or wash off, so the print does not have a separate lifespan from the garment. Programs routinely run the same sublimated set for three or four seasons.

cta: Send us your design, your colors and your roster. Design and proofing are free, and nothing prints until you have approved it.

title: Choosing Basketball Jersey Fabric for Florida Heat
description: Mesh, moisture-wicking or standard polyester — the answer depends on your building, not on your budget.
standfirst: Mesh is not simply the cool option and wicking is not simply the expensive one. They solve different problems, and picking wrong is why a team ends up hot in a jersey that was supposed to fix it.

paras: There are only two mechanisms available to a fabric, and every product on this site uses one of them.

Airflow. An open-weave mesh has thousands of deliberate gaps, and warm air leaves through them instead of collecting against the skin. This only works if there is air moving on the other side of the fabric. In a sealed hall with no ventilation there is very little for it to work with.

Moisture management. A wicking fiber is extruded with channels running along its length; liquid moves along those channels by capillary action to the outer face, where a much larger surface area lets it evaporate. This works whether or not the air is moving, which is exactly why it is the answer indoors.
sections.pull: Mesh moves heat when there is air to move it. Wicking moves sweat whether or not there is. Which one you need is a question about your building.

paras: Coastal Florida gets genuine air movement, even in August. Doors open onto a breeze and outdoor courts get real airflow, which is why an open weave earns its price in places like Tampa and the bay area more than it does further inland.

Inland cities do not. A gym in Orlando or Lakeland that has been closed overnight has still air inside it, and an open weave has nothing to work with. The wicking knit does more there, and it is what we recommend for Polk County indoor play almost every time.
Outdoors, mesh wins everywhere in the state. There is always some air movement outside, and the extra ventilation matters more when there is no building doing any of the work.

Before fabric, there is a bigger variable that most programs never consciously choose: how dark the jersey is. A dark ground absorbs considerably more radiant heat than a light one under direct sun, and no weave takes all of that back.

For an indoor season it barely matters — there is no radiant load in a gym. For a program playing regular outdoor fixtures it matters more than the fabric does, which is why plenty of teams run a light home kit outdoors and keep the dark set for indoor games.

If your identity is a dark color and your season is outdoors, the sensible compromise is ordering it in mesh. That is why we recommend an open-weave version of a dark jersey rather than talking a program out of its colors.
GSM is grams per square meter, and it is the closest thing to an objective weight figure. Our standard sublimation polyester is 155 GSM, the wicking knit is 145, and athletic mesh is 125.

Those gaps are smaller than they sound and more noticeable than they look on paper. Ten GSM is roughly the difference a guard reports in the fourth quarter of a fast game, which is why a thinner-gauge lightweight jersey exists as its own product rather than as a footnote.

The one figure that is not a trade-off is the wicking behavior, because it is structural rather than applied. A fabric that wicks because of how its fiber is built still wicks after a hundred washes; one treated with a topical finish stops within a season.

faqs.q: Is mesh always cooler than a closed knit?
faqs.a: Not always. Mesh works by letting heat escape through the weave, and that requires air moving past the fabric. In a sealed indoor gym with no ventilation there is very little air movement, and a moisture-wicking knit that moves sweat to an evaporating surface can do more. Outdoors, or in a hall with the doors open, mesh is clearly cooler.

faqs.q: Does the jersey color affect how hot a player gets?
faqs.a: Outdoors, significantly. A dark ground absorbs far more radiant heat from direct sun than a light one, and that is a property of the color rather than the fabric. Indoors it makes almost no difference, because there is no radiant load in a gym. Programs playing outdoor fixtures often run a light kit outdoors and a dark one inside.

faqs.q: What does GSM mean on a jersey?
faqs.a: Grams per square meter — the fabric's weight. Our standard sublimation polyester is 155 GSM, the moisture-wicking knit 145, and athletic mesh 125. The differences look small written down and are noticeable in the fourth quarter of a fast game.

faqs.q: Does moisture-wicking wear off?
faqs.a: Not on ours, because the wicking is structural. The fiber is extruded with channels along its length that move liquid by capillary action, so there is nothing applied that can wash away. Fabrics treated with a topical wicking finish do lose it, usually within a season, and fabric softener accelerates it on any of them.

cta: Tell us what your gym is like — conditioned, unconditioned, or outdoors. That one answer decides the fabric more than anything else.

title: What Actually Drives the Cost of Custom Basketball Jerseys
description: Design, colors, quantity, setup — which of these change the price of a custom basketball jersey and which do not.
standfirst: Most of the things people expect to pay extra for do not cost extra here. It is worth knowing which, because it changes what you should spend the budget on.

paras: Design is free, whether you send a finished vector logo, a photograph of last season's jersey, or nothing at all. So is the digital proof, and so are revisions to it — we would rather spend an extra day on a numeral outline than reprint a set.

Color count is free. Because the whole design is laid down in one pass rather than one screen per color, a twelve-color design with a gradient costs exactly what a two-color design costs. This is the single biggest difference from screen printing and the one most programs do not exploit.

Individual names are free, because each jersey is printed from its own file rather than a shared screen. Twelve different names cost what twelve identical jerseys cost. So does a different dedication on every back, which is why a fundraising jersey with individual dedications is not more expensive than a plain one.
Shipping within the United States is free, and there is no minimum order and no setup charge.
sections.pull: Design, proofs, revisions, color count, individual names, shipping, and setup: all zero. What you are paying for is the garment.

paras: Almost entirely the garment itself, which makes the pricing easy to reason about.
A plain single-color jersey is the cheapest finished thing we make — the saving is in the simpler layout, not in a cheaper cloth, since a plain jersey uses the same fabric as a full-design one.

A uniform set is roughly two garments, because it is two garments. A reversible is more again, because it is two complete jerseys bonded into one. Practice kit sits well below game kit for the same reason a plain jersey sits below a sublimated one: the layout is deliberately simpler.

Fabric moves the price a little. Mesh, wicking and standard polyester are close enough that we would not recommend choosing between them on cost — pick the one that suits your building and let the price follow.
The advice we give is nearly always the same, and it runs against instinct. Put the budget into practice kit and a straightforward game jersey rather than a detailed set.

A program practices around a hundred and fifty times and plays twenty-five games. Practice jerseys in two contrasting colors are what the squad actually wears, and they solve squad splits without a bag of pinnies nobody returns.

The design can get more ambitious next year without the kit stopping matching, because your color is matched once and stored. That is the part that makes a staged approach work rather than leaving you with two sets that do not sit together.

sections.h2: The one thing that does cost extra
paras: Rushing. Not as a surcharge — we do not add one — but as a constraint on what is possible. Production is the real limit, and it cannot be compressed past a point.

Which is why the useful thing to send with an enquiry is the date the kit is needed rather than the date you plan to order. We work backward from it and tell you the latest order date that makes it, or say plainly that it does not.

faqs.q: Do more colors cost more?
faqs.a: No. The entire design is printed in one pass rather than one screen per color, so color count does not affect the price at all. A twelve-color design with a gradient and a photographic fill costs exactly what a two-color design costs. This is the largest practical difference from screen printing.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum order?
faqs.a: No minimum and no setup charge. A team of eight pays the same per jersey as a school ordering thirty, because each jersey is printed individually rather than from a shared screen that has to be paid for regardless of run length.

faqs.q: Do individual player names cost extra?
faqs.a: No. Each jersey is printed from its own file, so twelve different names cost exactly what twelve identical jerseys cost. The same applies to individual dedications, different sponsors per jersey, or any other per-player variation.

faqs.q: Is there a rush charge?
faqs.a: No, but there is a limit. Production takes the time it takes and cannot be compressed indefinitely. Send us the date the kit is needed rather than the date you plan to order, and we will tell you the latest order date that still makes it — or say plainly that it does not.

cta: Send a quantity and a rough spec and we will price it properly. No minimum, no setup charge, and no per-color cost.

title: Practice Jerseys vs Game Jerseys: What Is Actually Different
h1: Practice Kit and Game Kit Are Not the Same Garment
description: A team practices 150 times and plays 25 games. Here is what changes between the two jerseys, and why buying one for both is a false economy.
standfirst: The jersey a program wears most is not the one it spends most on — and the two are built for genuinely different failure modes.

paras: A season is roughly twenty-five games and a hundred and fifty practices. That means the kit a program is seen in is a small fraction of the kit it actually wears, and yet the uniform budget almost always goes the other way round.

Which is fine, up to a point — a game jersey is a public-facing garment and should look like one. The mistake is treating practice kit as a cheaper version of the same thing rather than as a different product with different requirements.

Practice kit is judged on how it looks after fifty hot washes, not on how it photographs. So the knit is chosen for durability, the shoulder and side seams are double-needle stitched because that is where practice tops split, and the neckline is bound so it does not stretch into a loop by mid-season.

Game kit is judged on the opposite. Bound armholes that hold their line, a fabric with enough body to keep a formal look under arena lighting, and side panels that match the shorts — which only happens if the jersey and shorts are printed together from one color file.
The layout differs too. Practice jerseys keep to two colors and a number, deliberately, because that is what makes two per player affordable.
sections.pull: Buy game kit for how it looks in twenty-five games. Buy practice kit for how it looks after a hundred and fifty washes. Those are different specifications.

paras: In Florida humidity, kit that does not dry overnight goes back on damp the next day, and by October the whole pile smells regardless of how it is washed. That is what retires practice gear here — not wear, and not the print failing.

Two jerseys per player, alternated, ends it completely. The price of practice kit is set so that is a realistic order rather than an aspirational one, and a program buying one each is usually buying two each by January anyway.
It applies most to shorts, because the leg holds moisture longest, which is why practice shorts are priced for two pairs as a matter of course.

Order practice jerseys in two contrasting colors on one run. Half the roster in each, and five-on-five is set up in thirty seconds without a bag of pinnies that nobody returns and nobody wants to wear.
Numbers can repeat across the two colors, because practice kit answers to no league roster rule. One order covers scrimmage, drills and any split a coach wants to make, at one price and one delivery.

faqs.q: Can we just use old game jerseys for practice?
faqs.a: You can, and plenty of programs do, but it costs more over time than buying practice kit. A game jersey is built for twenty-five outings and a hundred and fifty washes will tell on it, particularly at the neckline and shoulder seams. Practice kit is built the other way round and costs less to begin with.

faqs.q: Why order two contrasting colors?
faqs.a: Because it splits a squad instantly. Half the roster in each color means five-on-five is set up in thirty seconds without pinnies, which get lost, smell, and nobody wants to wear twice. Numbers can repeat across the two colors because practice kit answers to no league roster rule.

faqs.q: Do practice jerseys need to match our game kit?
faqs.a: No, and trying to make them match usually means paying game-kit prices for practice gear. Most programs order practice kit in the team's base color with a simple accent, which reads as belonging to the program without needing to reproduce the game design panel for panel.

faqs.q: How many practice jerseys per player?
faqs.a: Two, if the budget allows it. Not for wear but for drying — in Florida humidity a jersey that does not dry overnight goes back on damp, and that is what makes a whole pile smell by October. Practice kit is priced so two per player is realistic.

cta: Order practice kit and game kit together and both come from one stored color, so they belong to the same program.

title: How to Care for Sublimated Basketball Jerseys
h1: Making a Jersey Last More Than One Season
description: What actually damages a sublimated jersey, what does not, and the one habit that matters most in Florida.
standfirst: Most jersey care advice is written for garments with something printed on the surface. Sublimated kit has different rules, and one of them is genuinely counter-intuitive.

paras: The color is inside the fiber rather than on it, which rules out most of what damages ordinary team kit. It cannot crack, peel, lift at an edge or wash off, because there is no layer to do any of those things.

A hot wash will not fade it. Neither will a tumble dryer, sunlight over a season, chlorine from a pool bag, or a parent who has never read a care label. That last one matters more than it sounds: the youth basketball jerseys we supply are laundered by a hundred different households, and no care instruction survives that.
It also will not transfer color. A red sublimated jersey will not pink a white wash, because the dye is bonded into the polymer rather than sitting loose on the surface.

Direct heat on the artwork. An iron is the one real risk, and the reason is exact: heat and pressure are what put the dye into the fiber, so heat and pressure can move it again. Never iron a sublimated panel. Nothing else in a laundry room comes close to a domestic iron's temperature.

Fabric softener. It leaves a film that dulls large color areas and, on a wicking fabric, coats the fiber channels that do the moisture work. On a moisture-wicking shirt this is the single worst thing you can do to it.
Bleach. On a sublimated garment, bleach attacks the dye rather than the stain, because the dye is the fabric. The result is a permanent pale patch.
sections.pull: Hot wash, tumble dry, leave it in the sun — all fine. Iron it once and you have a problem that cannot be undone.

paras: Dry it properly, and dry it fast. This is the one that actually decides whether a set survives a season here.

Kit that goes back on damp is what makes a whole pile smell by October, and in this humidity that happens faster than most programs expect. It is not a washing problem and no detergent fixes it — the fabric was never dry.

Air drying is faster than a machine in Florida air anyway, and it is better for the bound armhole and hem edges that hold a jersey's shape. Two garments per player, alternated, removes the problem entirely.

Salt carried in coastal air dries onto fabric as a pale residue. It cannot damage anything, but it shows — most on dark grounds and most of all on grey, which is one reason we suggest a wicking fabric whenever a program picks grey.

A cold wash the same day removes it completely. Leaving kit in a bag for a week is what turns a residue into a mark, which is the practical difference between coastal play and inland play as far as laundry is concerned.

faqs.q: Can I tumble dry a sublimated jersey?
faqs.a: Yes. The color is inside the fiber, so a dryer changes nothing about the print. Air drying is still preferable — it is faster than a machine in Florida air and gentler on the bound armhole and hem edges that keep a jersey's shape — but a dryer will not damage the design.

faqs.q: Why can't I iron it?
faqs.a: Because heat and pressure are exactly what put the dye into the fiber in the first place, and a domestic iron reaches the temperature where dye can move again. Everything else in a laundry room is well below that. If a jersey needs creases removed, hang it damp instead.

faqs.q: Does fabric softener really matter?
faqs.a: On a wicking fabric, very much. Softener leaves a film that coats the channels along each fiber — the structure that moves sweat to the outer face — so the fabric stops doing the thing you paid for. On standard polyester it is less serious but still dulls large color areas over a season.

faqs.q: What removes the salt marks from coastal play?
faqs.a: A cold wash the same day. Salt dries onto the fabric as a residue rather than bonding to it, so it rinses out easily if it has not been left for a week. It shows most on dark grounds and worst on grey.

cta: Every order ships with the care that suits its fabric. Ask us if you want it printed for a team handbook.

title: How to Measure a Basketball Team for Uniforms
description: The four measurements that matter, the two that do not, and what to do when half the squad cannot be measured in time.
standfirst: Most sizing problems are not measuring errors. They are habits carried over from cotton, applied to a fabric that behaves differently.

paras: Polyester does not shrink. It holds its dimensions through hot washes and a dryer, which is precisely why the color survives them too.

So there is no need to size up to allow for a first wash. That allowance is a cotton habit, and applied here it produces a jersey a full size too big for an entire season. Order the size you intend to wear.

The related habit worth dropping is sizing a whole roster from one chart. Height and chest disagree on roughly half of any group of players the same age, and where they disagree the chest wins for a top.
sections.pull: Order the size you want to wear. There is no shrinkage to allow for, and allowing for it anyway is the single most common sizing error we see.

paras: Chest decides the size of any top. Measure around the fullest point with the arms relaxed and the tape horizontal — not pulled tight, and not over a bulky layer unless the jersey will be worn over one.

Waist and hip decide shorts. Measure the natural waist where the band will actually sit, just above the hip bone rather than at the belly button, and the fullest part of the seat with feet together. The hip measurement decides comfort in a defensive stance more than the waist does, and it is the one most often skipped.

Sleeve length only matters on a long-sleeve garment, and there it decides the size outright. Measure from the center back of the neck, across the shoulder, to the wrist bone. A player with long arms is better one size up even when the chest says otherwise, because a sleeve that ends short of the wrist cannot be fixed.
Armhole depth matters if your competition specifies a maximum. It is the measurement most likely to fail a uniform check, and the cheapest to verify beforehand.

Order a size spread rather than a per-player list. A typical adult high-school spread runs Small through 2XL weighted toward Medium and Large, and because there is no minimum you can top up a single size later at the same per-unit price.

Where the squad genuinely cannot be measured, the faster route is often blanks. Undecorated jerseys ship in five to ten days because there is nothing to proof, and you can have them numbered locally the week the roster is final.
Youth sizing runs on height and chest together, and the cut already allows extra body length and a deeper armhole for exactly this reason.

Size up once for a season-long order. A jersey slightly large in November fits properly by February. Do not size up twice — two sizes large is a jersey that never fits and gets in the way all season, which is a different problem from the one you were solving.

For a whole league, send heights and weights with the quote and we size the roster at no charge. On a twelve-team youth uniform order that is several hours of somebody's evening that does not have to happen.

faqs.q: Should we size up to allow for shrinkage?
faqs.a: No. Polyester does not shrink — it holds its dimensions through hot washes and a dryer, which is why the color survives them too. Sizing up for shrinkage is a habit carried over from cotton and produces a jersey a full size too big for the whole season.

faqs.q: What if we cannot measure everyone in time?
faqs.a: Order a size spread rather than a per-player list — a typical adult high-school spread runs Small to 2XL weighted toward Medium and Large. There is no minimum, so you can top up a single size later at the same per-unit price. If the roster is genuinely unknown, blanks ship faster and can be numbered locally once the squad is final.

faqs.q: How do we size youth players for a whole season?
faqs.a: Size up once. The cut already allows extra body length and a deeper armhole, so a jersey slightly large in November fits properly by February. Do not size up twice — two sizes large is a jersey that never fits. Send heights and weights with your quote and we will size the roster at no charge.

faqs.q: Which measurement matters most for shorts?
faqs.a: The hip, and it is the one most often skipped. Measure the fullest part of the seat with feet together — it decides comfort in a defensive stance more than the waist does. The waist still sets the band size, but a player between sizes at the hip should size up.

cta: Send heights and weights with your enquiry and we will size every player on the roster at no charge.

title: Planning a Uniform Order Around a Fixed Date
description: Season openers, tournaments and awareness nights do not move. Here is how to order so the kit arrives before them.
standfirst: The single most useful thing you can send with an enquiry is not a design or a quantity. It is the date the kit is actually needed.

paras: Shipping is free and fast within the United States, and it is almost never what decides a delivery date. Production is.

Most jerseys run seven to fourteen business days. A full uniform set runs ten to sixteen, because it is two garments. A reversible runs twelve to eighteen, because it is two complete jerseys bonded into one — and that bonding is a step that cannot be hurried.
The fastest thing we make is a blank. Undecorated jerseys ship in five to ten days because there is no artwork stage and nothing to proof.

Design and proofing happen before production and are not included in those windows. If you send finished vector artwork the proof is quick; if we are designing from a brief, allow a few days for the first proof and a day or two for each round of revisions.

Revisions are free and unlimited, which is deliberate — but they are also the stage most likely to consume a week if a committee is approving the design. Nominating one person to approve the proof is the single biggest thing a program can do to protect its own date.

Color matching adds nothing to the timeline if you send a physical reference. It adds a round trip if we have to send a fabric swatch first, which is worth doing on a hard-to-match purple jersey — the color where screen and fabric disagree most.
sections.pull: Send the date the kit is needed, not the date you plan to order. We will work backward and tell you the latest date we can accept it and still make the game.

paras: Some orders have a fixture behind them rather than a season. An awareness night, a military appreciation game, a senior night, a hosted tournament — these are on a calendar that was set months ago and will not shift for a kit delivery.

For those we schedule backward from the fixture as a matter of course. October is the busiest month for awareness game jerseys, and November for appreciation kits, which is exactly when the queue is longest — so those enquiries want to arrive earlier than feels necessary.
If a date is not achievable we say so rather than accepting the order and hoping. That is more useful than the alternative, even though it is a worse sales conversation.
For a straightforward game jersey order with artwork supplied, four weeks from enquiry to delivery is comfortable and three is achievable.

For a full uniform set designed from a brief, allow five to six weeks. For a reversible set, six to seven. Add a week if the design has to be approved by more than one person, because it usually does.

faqs.q: How far ahead should we order for a season opener?
faqs.a: Four weeks is comfortable for a straightforward jersey order with artwork supplied, and three is achievable. A full uniform set designed from a brief wants five to six weeks, and a reversible set six to seven. Add a week if more than one person has to approve the design.

faqs.q: Do you charge for rush orders?
faqs.a: No, but we also cannot compress production past a point. Rather than a surcharge, we work backward from your date and tell you the latest date we can accept the order and still make it — or say plainly that it is not achievable, which is more useful than accepting and hoping.

faqs.q: What slows an order down most?
faqs.a: Proof approval. Revisions are free and unlimited, which is the right policy and also the stage most likely to consume a week when a committee is deciding. Nominating one person to approve the proof is the single biggest thing you can do to protect your own date.

faqs.q: What is the fastest option if the date is very close?
faqs.a: Blank jerseys — five to ten business days, because there is no artwork stage and nothing to proof. They arrive undecorated and can be numbered by a local shop once they land, which is often faster overall than a decorated order when the date is tight.

cta: Tell us the date first. We will tell you what is achievable before you commit to anything.

title: Ordering Youth Basketball Uniforms for Players Who Are Still Growing
description: The problem adult uniforms never have, and how the cut, the sizing and the ordering should change because of it.
standfirst: A set bought in October is worn by a slightly different child in March. A uniform that fits half a season is a uniform bought twice.

paras: A youth jersey is not simply an adult one scaled down. Ours carry extra length through the body and a slightly deeper armhole, and the shorts have a longer drawcord range so the waist can be taken in early and let out later.

None of that reads as oversized on day one, which is the point — a jersey visibly too big in November is a different problem from one outgrown by February. The neckline is bound rather than folded so it stays comfortable as shoulders broaden, which is a common reason a child quietly stops wearing kit.
A youth uniform set built this way is the difference between one order and two.
Youth sizing runs on height and chest together, and where the two disagree, follow the chest for a top and the waist for shorts.

Then size up once for a season-long order. That is the whole technique. Sizing up twice produces a jersey that never fits properly and gets in the way all season, which is a worse outcome than the one you were avoiding.
Send heights and weights with the quote and we size the roster at no charge. For a league ordering across an age range that is several hours of somebody's evening that does not have to happen.
sections.pull: One size up absorbs a season of growth. Two sizes up is a jersey nobody enjoys wearing for eight months.

paras: Youth kit is laundered by as many households as there are players, with as many habits, and no care label survives that. So it should not need one.

Because the color is inside the fiber rather than printed on the surface, a hot wash and a tumble dryer change nothing. There is no ritual for a parent to follow and nothing to go wrong. Fabric softener is the only thing worth avoiding, and it is not urgent.
It also will not transfer color — a red set will not pink a white wash — which removes the other question families ask.

We print youth numbers one size larger than adult kit as standard. It costs nothing at the print stage and it solves a real problem: a volunteer official or a parent in a community hall is reading from considerably further back than an official at a school arena's scorer's table.

For practice, the same logic goes further. Youth practice jerseys carry oversized numbers so a coach can call a player from the far baseline, and numbers may repeat across two colors because practice kit answers to no roster rule.

faqs.q: How much should we size up for a growing player?
faqs.a: One size, once. The cut already allows extra body length and a deeper armhole, so one size up absorbs a season of growth and fits properly by February. Two sizes up produces a jersey that never fits and gets in the way for eight months.

faqs.q: Will youth kit survive being washed by different families?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is designed to. The color is inside the fiber rather than printed on the surface, so a hot wash and a tumble dryer change nothing and there is no care ritual to follow. It will not transfer color either — a red set will not pink a white wash.

faqs.q: Why are youth numbers printed larger?
faqs.a: Because a community hall is read from further back than a school arena. A volunteer official or a parent is often twenty or thirty feet further from the floor than an official at a scorer's table, and the extra size costs nothing at the print stage.

faqs.q: Can a league order for every team at once?
faqs.a: Yes, and each team's colorway is stored separately so a replacement jersey in a later season matches the rest of that team's set. Sizes mix freely across the whole run and the delivery is sorted and labeled by team at no extra cost.

cta: Send heights and weights for the whole roster and we will size every player, at no charge.

title: League Uniform Rules and What They Mean for Your Jersey Design
description: Number height, sleeve requirements and color restrictions — the three uniform rules that fail a check, and when to confirm them.
standfirst: Nothing about a design is expensive to change at proof stage. Everything about it is expensive to change after printing, because the design is dyed into the fabric rather than applied to it.

paras: On a screen-printed or heat-pressed jersey, a number can be removed and replaced. It is not elegant, but it is possible.

On a sublimated jersey it is not. The dye is inside the fibre, so changing a number's height or a panel's color means printing the garment again from the start. That is the whole reason we push programmes to confirm their rules before approving a proof rather than after a first game.
sections.pull: A rule checked at proof stage costs nothing. The same rule discovered at a first game costs the whole order.

paras: Number height. Most competitions specify a minimum, and it usually differs between the front and the back. This is the single most common reason a uniform is sent back, and it is entirely preventable — the figure is in your rulebook and takes a minute to find.

Sleeve requirements. Some Florida districts and rec leagues require a sleeved uniform, and a sleeveless jersey will not pass whatever else it does well. If yours does, a sleeved competition jersey satisfies it without giving up shoulder range — and it is available in mesh if your venue is hot.

Contrast. Less often written into a rulebook and more often enforced in practice: an official who cannot read a number from the scorer's table will say so. A light numeral on a yellow or gold uniform is the classic failure, which is why we treat dark numerals there as a requirement rather than a style choice.

We proof numeral contrast at viewing distance rather than at desk distance, because a design that reads beautifully on a screen can be unreadable across a gym. That is the only distance that matters to an official.

Patterns get the same treatment. A camouflage design is engineered to break up shapes, and a jersey number is a shape that must not break up — so every camo jersey gets a solid number panel or a heavy contrast outline as standard.
What we cannot check is your rulebook. Send the number height and any sleeve or color restriction with your enquiry and it becomes part of the proof.
None of this applies to practice gear, and that is worth exploiting rather than forgetting. Numbers can repeat across a squad, sizes can be inconsistent, and colors need not match anything.
Which is exactly why ordering practice jerseys in two contrasting colors works: one run splits a squad for five-on-five with duplicate numbers and no rulebook to satisfy.

faqs.q: Can a number be changed after the jerseys arrive?
faqs.a: Not on a sublimated jersey. The dye is inside the fibre rather than applied on top, so changing a number's height or color means printing the garment again from scratch. This is why confirming your league's rules before approving the proof matters more here than it would with a heat-pressed number.

faqs.q: Which rule causes the most reprints?
faqs.a: Number height. Most competitions specify a minimum and it often differs between front and back, and it is the most common reason a uniform is sent back. The figure is in your rulebook and takes a minute to find — send it with your enquiry and it becomes part of the proof.

faqs.q: Do sleeve requirements vary?
faqs.a: Yes, by league and by classification. Some Florida districts and rec leagues require a sleeved uniform and a sleeveless jersey will not pass, whatever else it does. If your rules permit sleeveless, that cut is cooler and gives more shoulder range, so it is worth checking rather than assuming.

faqs.q: Do practice jerseys have to follow the same rules?
faqs.a: No. Practice kit answers to no roster rule, so numbers may repeat across a squad and colors need not match your game set. That is what makes ordering two contrasting colors on one run the standard way to split a squad without pinnies.

cta: Send your league's number height and any sleeve rule with the enquiry. It becomes part of the proof and cannot then be missed.

title: Number and Name Legibility on a Basketball Jersey
description: Contrast, outline weight, font choice and pattern — what decides whether a number carries from the baseline.
standfirst: Size is the part everyone gets right. Contrast is the part that fails, and it fails at distance rather than on a screen.

paras: A large number in a color close to its background is harder to read at thirty feet than a smaller number in a color far from it. This is not intuition — it is how the eye resolves edges, and it is why contrast is the first thing we check.

The classic failures are predictable. White on yellow or gold. Mid-blue on mid-purple. Any accent color on a bright orange ground that sits close to it on the wheel. Each of those looks fine at desk distance and disappears from the bleachers.
An outline is not decoration. It is a second edge in a contrasting color, and on a mid-tone ground it is often what makes a numeral resolve at all.

Weight matters more than presence. A hairline outline adds nothing at distance; a heavy one holds the shape even when the fill and the ground are close in value. On a busy design an outline can carry a number that would otherwise be lost.

This is the whole technique behind patterned kit. Camouflage is designed to break up shapes, so a camo basketball jersey gets either a solid panel behind the numeral or a heavy contrast outline, and we proof it at viewing distance to check.
sections.pull: We proof numbers at bleacher distance, not desk distance. A design that reads on a monitor and not from the stands has failed at the only distance that counts.

paras: Block and varsity faces exist in team sport because they resolve at distance — heavy strokes, open counters, unambiguous digits. A condensed or decorative face can look sharper up close and lose a 3 against an 8 at thirty feet.
The digits worth checking are 3 and 8, 6 and 5, and 1 and 7. If your chosen face makes any of those pairs similar, it will cost somebody a call at some point in the season.

A player name is read from far closer than a number and by people who already know it, so contrast matters less and character matters more. It is the one place a distinctive face is a reasonable choice.

Names cost nothing to add, because each jersey is printed from its own file rather than a shared screen. Twelve different names cost exactly what twelve identical jerseys cost, which is also why individual dedications on awareness kit are free.

faqs.q: Is a bigger number always more readable?
faqs.a: No. Contrast decides legibility at distance more than size does — a large number in a color close to its background is harder to read at thirty feet than a smaller one in a color far from it. White on yellow is the classic failure, and it fails no matter how large it is printed.

faqs.q: Does the outline actually help?
faqs.a: Yes, and its weight matters more than its presence. An outline is a second edge in a contrasting color, and on a mid-tone ground it is often what makes a numeral resolve at all. A hairline outline adds nothing at distance; a heavy one holds the shape even when fill and ground are close in value.

faqs.q: How do you make numbers readable on a patterned jersey?
faqs.a: Either a solid panel printed behind the numeral or a heavy contrast outline, and usually both on a busy pattern. Camouflage in particular is engineered to break up shapes, and a number is a shape that must not break up. We proof those designs at viewing distance rather than on a screen.

faqs.q: Do player names cost extra?
faqs.a: No. Each jersey is printed from its own file rather than a shared screen, so twelve different names cost exactly what twelve identical jerseys cost. The same applies to individual dedications or a different sponsor on each jersey.

cta: Send your number height and font preference and we will proof it at the distance an official actually reads it from.

title: Choosing Team Colors That Reproduce Correctly on Fabric
h1: Why the Color on Your Screen Is Not the Color
description: Screens build color from light, fabric builds it from dye, and the two disagree most on exactly the colors teams pick.
standfirst: Almost every disappointed delivery we hear about traces back to one thing: a color chosen from a screenshot rather than from something physical.

sections.h2: Two different ways to make a color
paras: A screen makes color by adding light — red, green and blue emitters at varying intensity. Fabric makes color by absorbing it: dye removes wavelengths and what bounces back is what you see. These are opposite processes, and the ranges they can reach do not fully overlap.
The consequence is specific rather than general. Some colors cross the gap almost perfectly; others do not, and they are unfortunately the ones sports teams choose most.

Purple is the worst. Screens build it from red and blue light and fabric builds it from dye, and a purple chosen on a phone frequently prints noticeably more blue, or more maroon, than expected. If you take one thing from this piece, send a physical chip for any purple basketball jersey.

Orange is next, and it is the color we are asked for most in Florida. A bright orange on a monitor often prints duller or browner than expected, which is why we match it against a physical reference and never a screenshot.

Red reproduces well but varies. Small differences in dye load shift it between orange-red and blue-red — invisible on one jersey and obvious across twelve hanging together, which is why a custom red uniform set has its jersey and shorts printed in one run.

Green is not hard to print but is hard to specify. Forest, hunter, kelly, emerald and lime are five identities rather than five shades, and a supplier treating them as interchangeable is how a school ends up with the wrong one.
sections.pull: Send a Pantone chip, a printed style guide, or a jersey you already own. A phone photograph has passed through a camera, a display and compression before it reaches us.

sections.h2: What to send, in order of usefulness
paras: A Pantone value is best — it is a standard, and it means the same thing to everyone. A printed school style guide is nearly as good. A physical garment you already own is excellent, because it is the actual target.
A photograph is the weakest, and a screenshot of a website is the weakest of all, because it has already been compressed twice and displayed on a screen calibrated to nothing in particular.
Where a color is critical and you have no standard reference, ask for a fabric swatch before committing to a large run. It adds a round trip and settles the question completely.
The failure that costs most is not the first order. It is the third — a replacement jersey two seasons later that arrives a half-shade off, so the player wearing it looks like a substitute.

That happens when a color is re-judged by eye on each reorder rather than stored. Ours is matched once against your physical reference and kept against the account, so a year-three jersey prints from the same file as the year-one run.
It matters most for leagues. On a twelve-team youth uniform order each team's colorway is stored separately, which is what makes a single replacement possible at all.

faqs.q: Why does the color look different from my screen?
faqs.a: Because a screen makes color by adding light and fabric makes it by absorbing it, and the ranges those two processes can reach do not fully overlap. Purple and orange sit furthest apart, which is why we match those from a physical reference rather than from a screen value.

faqs.q: What is the best color reference to send?
faqs.a: A Pantone value, because it means the same thing to everyone. A printed style guide is nearly as good, and a garment you already own is excellent because it is the actual target. A screenshot is the weakest reference there is.

faqs.q: Which colors are hardest to get right?
faqs.a: Purple first, then orange, then red. Purple shifts most between screen and fabric. Orange frequently prints duller or browner than a monitor suggests. Red reproduces well but varies with dye load, so it must be printed in one run across a set.

faqs.q: Will a reorder next season match?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the original was matched from a physical reference. The value is stored against your account and reprinted from, rather than re-judged by eye each time. Re-judging is how a set drifts across three seasons into two visibly different shades.

cta: Send a Pantone value or a physical sample with your enquiry and we will match it once and store it for every season after.

title: Reversible Basketball Jerseys: When They Are Worth It
h1: Two Kits in One, and What It Costs
description: Reversibles halve the bag and the budget, and they are the warmest garment on the site. Both facts matter.
standfirst: A reversible is the clearest value proposition in team kit and the one most often bought for the wrong season.

paras: Two complete jerseys bonded back to back. Turn it inside out and the light home top becomes the dark away top, same player, same number, opposite color.

For any programme that needs both colors and can fund one set, that is the whole argument — and it is a strong one. A reversible jersey costs substantially less than two single-layer jerseys, and it is one order, one colour match and one delivery rather than two.

sections.h2: The part that is genuinely harder to make
paras: Both faces have to be fully finished, which is the easy half. The difficult half is that the numbers on each side must sit in register with each other, or the away number shows as a shadow behind the home number under arena lighting.

The second difficulty is opacity. A light home face over a dark away face will ghost badly if the bond and the layer weights are wrong. Ours are bonded across the whole panel rather than only at the seams — an edge-bonded reversible bubbles in the middle of the chest after a season, and it cannot be repaired.
The third is the edges. Every armhole and hem is bound, because those are the two points pulled every time the garment is turned, and an unbound edge on a bonded double layer curls apart.
sections.pull: A reversible is the hardest garment here to build properly, and the easiest to build badly. Ghosting numbers and curling armholes are what a cheap one looks like by February.

paras: Two bonded layers weigh 240 GSM against a single layer's 155, and no fabric choice changes that. It is the warmest garment on this site.

In an air-conditioned arena that is unnoticeable. In an unconditioned Florida hall in August, or on an outdoor court, a player will feel it — and we would rather say so than sell around it. For those venues an open-weave mesh jersey is a far more comfortable answer.
Plenty of programmes run both: reversibles through tournament season and single-layer kit for the hot months, printed from the same stored color so the two sets belong together.
The garment that solves home and away also splits a squad instantly. Turn half the roster inside out and five-on-five is set up, with no pinnies at all.

That makes a reversible genuinely useful at practice as well as on a tournament Saturday, which is worth weighing against a separate set of two-color practice jerseys — though practice kit is still cheaper and tougher for daily use.

faqs.q: How much does a reversible save against two jerseys?
faqs.a: Substantially — it is one garment rather than two, one color match, one order and one delivery. It costs more than a single jersey because it is two complete jerseys bonded together, but far less than buying home and away separately.

faqs.q: Do reversibles run hot?
faqs.a: Yes. Two bonded layers are 240 GSM against a single layer's 155, which makes it the warmest garment we sell. In a conditioned arena that is unnoticeable; in an unconditioned Florida hall in August or on an outdoor court, a player will feel it. For those venues a mesh jersey is far more comfortable.

faqs.q: What makes a cheap reversible look cheap?
faqs.a: Two things, and both show by February. Numbers out of register, so the away number appears as a shadow behind the home number under arena lighting. And unbound edges, which curl apart at the armhole and hem — the two points pulled every time the garment is turned.

faqs.q: Can we use reversibles for practice as well?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a genuine second use — turn half the roster inside out and five-on-five is set up without pinnies. Dedicated practice jerseys are still cheaper and tougher for daily use, but a reversible covers both jobs if the budget only stretches to one.

cta: Tell us your venues and your season. If a reversible is the wrong answer for your gym, we will say so.
